newsitem.title: USA: Florida pension fund to unload tobacco stocks.
newsitem.headline: Florida pension fund to unload tobacco stocks.

text.p: Florida pension fund trustees Wednesday ordered portfolio managers to divest the estimated $825 million of tobacco stocks in the $60 billion retirement fund covering state workers.
No timetable was set for selling the stocks, but a state pension official said the divestment would be carried out as quickly as possible without hurting share prices.
Tom Herndon, executive director of the state pension agency, said the portofolio managers did not want to shake up Wall Street with the sales and declined to discuss specifics of the divestiture.
"Number one, I don't have an answer," Herndon told reporters asking about the timing of stock sales.

"But, more importantly, I don't want to tell the whole world what our decision will be. We don't want to make the market here. We don't want to drive the prices on these stocks because of our behaviour. Even if we had a specific game plan in mind this morning, I would not disclose that."

The vote of the three-member board of trustees was two to one. The dissenter was state Comptroller Robert Milligan, a Republican, who voted against Gov. Lawton Chiles and Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson, both Democrats.

Nelson described tobacco stocks as "too risky" and said, "With all the lawsuits, the talk of more government regulation, they are very unstable. Holding onto them would be contrary to the best financial interests of the members of the Florida Retirement System."

Nelson, who spent a year studying the divestment proposal pushed by anti-tobacco activist Chiles, said negotiations between tobacco companies and state governments suing them had fundamentally changed the prospects for the cigarette makers.
In the past three years Chiles has led an anti-tobacco crusade, which includes a high-profile lawsuit seeking to recover state spending on smoking-related illnesses.
Trial of the suit is scheduled to begin August 4.
Milligan said he voted against divestment because tobacco shares are good investments and the order to divest hinders the fund's professional managers.
"We're tying their hands in a manner that very well may not be solely in the interest of the...(pension fund) participants," he said.
According to Herndon, who oversees the fund covering 600,000 current government employees and 153,000 retirees, about 70 percent of Florida's tobacco investment is in Philip Morris Cos. Inc.

Tobacco company stocks fell marginally. Philip Morris lost 12.5 cents to $43.875, RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., parent of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., fell 25 cents to $32.50, and Loews Corp. lost 25 cents to $96.25, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
